tc33d00fa: Have you ever walked into a school toilet and the lights came on by themselves? Or noticed that street lamps only switch on when it gets dark? Those are examples of **smart lighting** — lights with sensors that switch themselves on and off.
t11d598e2: Smart lighting can save a lot of energy in some rooms and almost nothing in others. The key is to match the technology to how the room is actually used. This worksheet has tasks at three levels — Basic, Medium and Advanced. Your teacher will tell you which level to work on.
t5062fea7: A **smart light** has a small electronic "brain" and at least one sensor. The brain decides when to switch the light on or off based on what the sensor measures.
td71ac39c: **Motion sensor** — detects movement. The light turns on when somebody walks in and turns off again after a few minutes without movement.
td2d14a0a: **Daylight sensor** — measures how bright it is. The light turns on (or brightens) when it gets dark and turns off (or dims) when there is enough daylight.
tf45c77be: The two sensors save energy in different ways. A motion sensor saves energy in rooms that are sometimes used and sometimes empty (toilets, corridors, storerooms). A daylight sensor saves energy in rooms with windows, where the lights are often on while the sun is shining.
t07ad51cf: **Occupancy ratio** is the share of "lights on" hours that are actually needed. A storeroom that is lit for 4 hours but used for only 0.5 hours has an occupancy ratio of 12.5 % — so up to 87.5 % of the energy could be saved. A classroom that is lit for 8 hours and used for 6 hours has a ratio of 75 % — only 25 % can be saved.
t42eadb06: **Time-out delay:** a motion sensor waits 3–15 minutes after the last movement before it switches off, so the light does not go out when you sit still. Rule of thumb: real "lights on" time ≈ 1.2 × occupied time.

t2f5082ba: Step 4: Payback: €40 ÷ €39 per year ≈ 1 year. A very good investment.

te1b7a840: Modern school buildings often use **networked** smart lighting: every light can be controlled on its own, sensors share data, and the lighting works together with ventilation (HVAC) and the school timetable. This makes bigger savings possible — but it also raises new questions about complexity, privacy and data.

tb88095f5: Top view of a classroom. The windows are at the bottom and the whiteboard is on the left.
tb378bc3c: Zone 1: the row of lights nearest the windows. Sensor: daylight, with manual override. Logic: dim to keep 300 lux on the desks. On sunny days these lights may run at 20 % power; on dark winter mornings at 100 %.
t31cddcf6: Zone 2: the row of lights furthest from the windows. Sensor: motion + timetable. Logic: on during scheduled lessons, motion-controlled outside lesson times, off otherwise.
t5615fd48: Zone 3: the light above the whiteboard. Separate switch for the teacher. Logic: always available, never automatic.
t935552a7: Estimated saving compared with "everything on": 35–45 %, depending on the weather and how the room is used.
